Guest Column

Institutionalizing the Psychoanalysis of Culture and Society: Psycho-Social Studies at the University of the West of England

Simon Clarke and Paul Hoggett

Paul Hoggett

Paul Hoggett   Professor of Politics at the University of the West of England and is currently training as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist. His research interests focus on the contribution that psychoanalytic theory (specifically post-Kleinian) can make to understanding the dynamics of political practice—struggle, innovation, and dialogue. He is co-editor of Organisational and Social Dynamics, a new journal arising from the Tavistock Group Relations tradition, the first issue of which will be published in June 2001. His books include Partisans in an Uncertain World (1992) and Emotional Life and the Politics of Welfare (2000).

Introduction

The Psycho-Social Studies Group at the University of the West of England, Bristol, encompasses a wide range of research interests and theoretical positions that share in common a commitment to psychoanalytic and other nonrationalist understandings of the human subject. We are also concerned with the application of such perspectives to organizational, social, and political issues and with the mutual influencing of psychoanalysis and contemporary social and political theory. Finally, some of the group are interested in the history of psychoanalysis and allied disciplines, such as Group Relations, and with the development of the therapeutic culture.

As we see it, psycho-social studies bridge the gap between theory and practice—several of the group are experienced Group Relations consultants, one is in training as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist, and some have been involved practically in politics. We are not interested in theorizing for the sake of it, losing sight of the human phenomena that we were studying. This may seem an obvious point, but often sociologists and political scientists get embroiled in their theoretical positions, whether Marxist, Weberian, or Durkheimian, and the social phenomena about which they are writing seem to take second place or are even forgotten about altogether.

A psycho-social approach links society, structure, and affect in a way that sociology, psychology, and social psychology have been largely unable to do. Structure and affect, the social and the psyche, are inseparable in terms of the explanation of social phenomena. This calls for a huge change in the way we think about research methods—how we know and how we can come to know about the world. There is thus an emphasis on the psychodynamic, the way in which the internal and external worlds are mediated by the group and individual and connect in ways that enable us to make sense of, think about, and exist in the world.

A psycho-social perspective, therefore, insists on the meaningfulness of human phenomena and experience, and their communicative nature, irrespective of whether the phenomenon in question is an impulsive act of violence, a bodily condition such as anorexia, or an apparently nonsensical and repetitive act. While it seeks the connections between body, psyche, and society, it also recognizes the irreducibility of any one of these domains vis-à-vis the others. It eschews all forms of reductionism and, as such, constitutes a challenge to sociological imperialism as much as to the psychological or medical/biological. Because no single discipline can hope to offer an adequate explanation, the psychosocial perspective is truly interdisciplinary and may enable us to start thinking in a different way about social problems and their possible solutions.

The Exposed Phallus/Penis

Women's movements since the early '60s, along with the various feminist ideologies that they spawned, from the most conservative (e.g., “real women”) to the most radical (e.g., radical and trans-gendered feminism), have certainly placed masculinity into a state of crisis. Crisis, perhaps is not the most advantageous word to use here, since masculinity, like femininity, is a concept that has only adventitious relations to biological sex; its various manifestations collectively constitute cultural, social, and psychosexual expressions of gender. Feminized masculinity and masculinized femininity are ultimately cultural achievements: recall Freud's claim that the polymorphous sexuality of the child has to be marked, mapped, and written on the body as it passes through the structures of Oedipalization. For Lacan, “sex” itself belongs to the psychic register of the Real—that is, to a place beyond language—because language “fails” in its attempt to articulate it once and for all. “Sex” constitutes a primary fantasy of identification that can only resolve itself “performatively,” to use the more contemporary language of Judith Butler, through the defiles of the signifier in their positive (hetero) and (sic) negative (homo) forms of Oedipalization. Consequently, there will always be “gender trouble.” In brief, the sex/gender of masculinity, like femininity, as enthnographers and anthropologists make transculturally evident, is some-“thing” to be acquired, achieved and initiated into, and this often involves painful mutilation and humiliating rituals.

The question remains open, however, why the Western myth of Oedipalization and its accompanying kinship structure must install the transcendental signifier of the phallus as the object of desire to make up for the fallible ontological lack each of us must face when we become enculturated into society. The phallus (⊘) insures that the paternal principle of the Law—a Law based on the exchange of women—and the orderly transmittance of the Symbolic Order from father to son become operable. This is the heart of what is taken to be the “classic” formulation of masculinity since perhaps the Chalcolithic age:1 a putative masculine norm that is phallic, virile, martial, and intensely Oedipalized which today has been exposed by feminists for its “penile pump,” not only in sport shoes but also in the gym. So why not identify the phallus as just one more metaphor among others for such an irreducible lack, i.e., for the Law of universal castration? Thus far, it seems such a theoretical attempt has not happened. The incest taboo has yet to be conceptualized outside the context of the phallogocentric order despite the best efforts of feminist theoreticians like Luce Irigaray.

Anti-Semitism in Russia: Some Interactions of Paranoia and Masochism in the Ethnic Realm1

Daniel Rancour-Laferriere

Daniel Rancour-Laferriere

Daniel Rancour-Laferriere   Professor of Russian and Director of the Russian Program at the University of California, Davis, and is the author of numerous books on Russia and the Russians, including The Slave Soul of Russia: Moral Masochism and the Cult of Suffering (1995) and Tolstoy on the Couch: Misogyny, Masochism, and the Absent Mother (1998).

Jews as the Prime Target of Ethnic Hatred in Russia

Anti-Semitism has been manifested in multifarious ways in Russia for as long as that nation has existed. From the late eighteenth century until the Bolshevik coup in 1917, most of Russia's Jews were restricted to living in a circumscribed area termed the “Pale of Settlement” (“cherta osedlosti evreev”). Many Jews managed to leave the Pale and migrate to other parts of the empire, but they were subjected to periodic expulsions from forbidden areas, and it was not until the fall of the tsarist government that this form of apartheid was fully eliminated. Meantime, Jews were subjected to quotas in admission to various public institutions, they were barred from the civil service and the officer corps, and they were in danger of having their property vandalized or destroyed, and of being beaten and killed in what were called pogroms. In the press they were vilified as economic exploiters of ethnic Russians. All of this was in addition to the ordinary, everyday anti-Semitism of Russian life—insults, ethnic slurs, and occasional physical assaults.

Later, during the Soviet period, everyday anti-Semitism remained alive and well in Russia. Beyond that, the horrendous pogroms of 1918-1921 took a minimum of 50,000 lives (although most of the perpetrators in this case were probably Ukrainian, not Russian). Jews were also victimized by Stalin's anti-Semitic machinations, including the arrest of members of the Jewish Anti-Fascist Committee as well as the arrest of alleged perpetrators of a “Doctors' Plot” against Soviet leaders. Soviet Jews would have been deported en masse to the east if Stalin had not died in 1953. The campaigns against “cosmopolitanism” and “Zionism” were essentially a government-sanctioned form of anti-Semitism. The reality of the Holocaust—including the fact that Russians, Ukrainians, and other Soviet citizens aided the German invaders in exterminating Jews—was played down or even falsified by Soviet historians. These unpleasant realities of Russian history have been extensively documented (for example: Rogger; Pinkus; Löwe; Weinerman; Dawidowicz; Dreizin; Pipes).

I still have difficulty seeing John F. Kennedy clear.

—T. H. White

He is a hero. And yet he is a void.

—Norman Mailer

Opening Reflections

A few years after its initial impact had been felt, Norman Mailer suggested that his pre-election, pro-Kennedy anthem, “Superman comes to the Supermarket,” could have been called “Filling the Holes in No Man's Land” (Presidential Papers 25). He noted that “American politics is rarely interesting for its men, its ideas, or the style of its movements. It is usually more fascinating in its gaps, its absences, its uninvaded territories” (25). Mailer's assessment of the mapped territory, of what was known, was bleak and biting. Instead of clearly defined dialectics and debates about vital principles, America had been swallowed by “the spirit of the supermarket, that homogenous extension of stainless surfaces and psychoanalyzed people … liv[ing] in the rootless pleasure world of an adult child” (32). Politics needed an “existential act” to penetrate and rip through all that flat, bland sameness—some rough reconsideration of what had been taken for granted, a rude or even obscene assault on harmony which could return us to that “subterranean river of untapped, ferocious, lonely and romantic desires, that concentration of ecstasy and violence which is the dream life of the nation” (38). In 1960, and despite his “doubts, … disquiets, and … certain distastes for Kennedy's dullness of mind” (27), Mailer saw in JFK a “potentiality to excite,” a sexual and visceral disavowal of the Eisenhower emptiness—so, as he writes in his collection of essays from the Kennedy years, he set about to get the man elected, to support the seductions of “personality” politics:

It was a hero America needed, a hero central to his time, a man whose personality might suggest contradictions and mysteries, which could reach into the alienated circuits of the underground, because only a hero can capture the secret imagination of his nation; a hero embodies the fantasy and so allows each private mind the liberty to consider its fantasy and find a way to grow. (41-42)

Monuments and Melancholia

Rico Franses

Rico Franses

Rico Franses   Currently living in New York, received his Ph.D. in Art History from the Courtauld Institute of Art, University of London. His book, Symbols, Meaning, Belief: The Giver and The Gift in Byzantine Art, will be published shortly. He published an earlier article on the theme of memorials, “Post-Monumentality: Frame, Grid, Space, Quilt,” in The Rhetoric of the Frame, ed. Paul Duro (1996).

Memorials always exist in a fraught relation to fear of disappearance: information stored solely as memory has a tenuous existence. Once forgotten, it has disappeared forever. Memorials always articulate this anxiety of forgetfulness when recollection has been instituted as a moral duty.

The solution the memorial adopts in its battle against ephemeral memory is an old one: it externalizes the information by recording it in some physically enduring form. Traditional formats of the monument, including the statue of a soldier and the plinth listing the names of the dead, demonstrate two types of such preservation. The heroic statue captures and stores the image of the fallen, while the inscribed names capture the words by which they are known. Of these, the name is infinitely more effective in serving the purpose of recollection than the generalized image. This is because the sound of the name of a person one knows is instantly evocative of a whole range of memories and associations concerning that person. Names seem to have the ability to cover the entire breadth of a person's behavior and character, as well as one's own interaction with them. They appear to function as the agglutinative center around which all the complexities of personhood gather, designating a core identity, yet accommodating an infinitely wide range of associations concerning the person. In the memorial, these qualities of individual specification and character summation appear to ensure the eternal memory of the person in question.

There is, however, a crucial problem concerning the use of names which radically affects their performance in the memorial. There exists a fundamental asymmetry in relation to the evocative quality of names which relates to whether or not, upon hearing a name, one is acquainted with its bearer. If one has no acquaintance with the named person, then the mention of his or her name will bear almost no connotations, and the manifold suggestions of the person's subjecthood, so easily encompassed within the sweep that a name executes, will be absolutely lacking. Acquaintance with the named person is the razor which will determine whether names will prove to be intensely meaningful to a listener or not. It follows from this that the function which a naming memorial performs will differ radically according to whether the observers of that memorial knew those to whom it refers. Names in a memorial may produce a flood of associations, and profoundly fulfil their function of evocation upon acquaintances of the dead, yet cannot have anything like this effect upon those to whom the dead are strangers. In its ostensive function of reminding us “lest we forget,” a stranger-memorial can have very little effect of remembrance, as there is no sense of the person who is lost, to be forgotten.

On the Insane Origin of Sanity

Shlomo Mendlovic

Shlomo Mendlovic

Shlomo Mendlovic   Psychiatrist at the Shalvata Mental Health Center and holds a Ph.D. in immunology from the Weizmann Institute of Science, Israel. He is interested in the relationship between psychiatry, sociology, and philosophy and in basic research that focuses on the mind-body enigma. He actively conducts large-scale studies in these subjects.

Introduction

In the name of medicine, modern society strips the mentally ill of their freedom, turns them into outcasts, and forces treatment

113

upon them—often against their will. Much has been written about the role insanity plays in defining sanity (Goffman; Miller Brown; Szasz; Foucault), and on the possibility that sanity generates insanity (Laing, Divided Self). The purpose of this study is to demonstrate that due to its uniqueness, insanity can revitalize society with innovative patterns that are not readily available to the sane. As such, this essay suggests that insanity be perceived not as the negative of sanity, but rather as alternative expecting to be realized.

Society and the Individual

Society, as an infrastructure that integrates individuals into an organized general body, is called upon to implement various unifying measures. The most important of these is the definition of social goals and delineation of basic ethical norms. The social goals and norms delineate the individual's path and act as a focus of attraction for a person's actions. Beyond the goals and norms, society has woven an extensive net of prohibitions designed to distance the individual from activities that are apt to harm the delicate social fabric. Such are prohibitions against incest, which prevent the corruption of the family structure, prohibitions against theft, which protect the individual's property, and so on. The system of social prohibitions acts as a mean of cohesion: as the individuals distance themselves from prohibitions, they draw themselves closer to the permitted. When the positive and negative cohesive methods fail, society reacts by implementing sanctions, whose strength is in direct proportion to the degree of deviation from the desired and permissible. Thus, minor deviations are dealt by warnings and monetary punishments, while in more severe cases, which either threaten the fabric of society or substantially disturb morality, more stringent methods are taken. Then, sanctions are designed to educate the individual while at the same time acting as deterrent for all. The most striking of these sanctions is prison, and the most stringent is the death penalty. The latter is implemented in a situation in which deterrence of the general public is so vital and pressing that society relinquishes its attempt to rehabilitate the individual as well as the principal of the sanctity of life.

However “tarnished” the origins of psychoanalysis now seem to us by their interest in the “savage” and the “primitive,” to assume that this material's recovery releases the unconscious from inquiry is, I think, a grave mistake. It implies that prejudice operates according to conscious and rational precepts, and that we can reach a level of self- and group understanding that is free of psychic ambivalence. (13)

So writes Christopher Lane in his introduction to The Psychoanalysis of Race, an anthology of essays that attempts to bring a Freudian rigor to postcolonial and antiracist criticism. He certainly has his work cut out for him, but all those embarrassing references to savages in the Freudian oeuvre are the least of his problems. The importance of psychological inquiry into racism goes without saying, but Lane still has to contend with the dubious validity of psychoanalysis as a science, not to mention the tendency among theorists of postcolonialism to regard psychoanalysis as too apolitical and ahistorical to be of much use. One can see the polemical steam boiling out of this book's ears every time the word ahistorical is mentioned.

Reading Wong Foo: Drag Queens in the English Classroom

Betty-Anne Schlender

Betty-Anne Schlender

Betty-Anne Schlender   Recently completed doctoral studies in the Department of Secondary Education at the University of Alberta. She is interested in psychoanalytic theories as they help to illuminate two areas of investigation: sex/gender as it relates to the reader-text exchange, and the process by which pre-service teachers' construction of an identity that incorporates “self-as-teacher” informs and is informed by representations of teachers in popular culture.

“Her Son is a Freak”: The Problem of Sex/Gender1

“Doc” (a pseudonym) is a male student in grade eleven who attended an urban high school in Alberta during the time I was investigating the ways that sex/gender influences, and is influenced by, the texts that we ask adolescents to read and interpret in our classrooms. Doc was enrolled in English 23, which in Alberta fulfills requirements for a high school diploma and is designed for those students who are not university-bound. I showed the movie To Wong Foo, Thanks for Everything! Julie Newmar (1995) to Doc and his classmates and asked them to respond to several scenes in writing. In one scene, Vida (Patrick Swayze), who is a drag queen and dressed as a woman, is rejected by her/his mother, apparently because Vida has chosen to deny the unambiguous and “natural” sex/gender identity into which s/he was born. When I asked students for their comments at this point in the movie, Doc wrote:

I feel sorry for the mother because her son is a Freak. His mom doesn't acceptate it. that doesn't mean she doesn't still love him. If he had the guts he would go see his family . And try and work things out.2

Doc's response to this scene—the emotions it evokes that cause him to label Vida “a Freak” (underlined for emphasis) and to mention the “guts” required to confront difficult family issues—is immediate, strongly worded, and apparently deeply felt. Unlike most of his classmates, who viewed the scene from Vida's perspective and felt a great deal of sympathy for her/him, Doc's sympathy lies with the mother, presumably because he shares at least some of her anxiety/confusion/revulsion toward a man who masquerades as a woman. Doc reads the scene in a way that ignores what others interpret as evidence that Vida did display “the guts” to visit her/his family and has made the difficult first move to “try and work things out.”

English teachers generally pride themselves on helping students to become more sophisticated in both processing and producing texts (whether these texts are in a print, film, electronic, or other format). Particularly in senior high school English classes, instruction, discussion, and assignments focus students' attention almost exclusively on analysis and criticism of the text. We do not routinely ask students to turn their attention from the text to themselves in order to notice and question the meaning of an affective response evoked by a text. This is true even though, for most of us, the reasons that a text grabs us, moves us, or shifts our construction of ourselves or the world in minor or important ways lie more in the idiosyncratic and unconscious desires, fantasies, and resistances which a text draws on and less in the artistry of the work itself.

The Best Teacher in America Stands and Delivers: The Case of Jaime Escalante

Jan Jagodzinski

Jan Jagodzinski

Jan Jagodzinski   Professor in the Department of Secondary Education, University of Alberta, in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, where he teaches visual art education and curricular issues as they relate to postmodern concerns of gender politics, culture studies, and media (film and television). He is a founding member of the Caucus on Social Theory in Art Education, editor of JSTAE (Journal of Social Theory in Art Education), past president of SIG Media, Culture and Curriculum, and author of The Anamorphic I/i; Postmodern Dilemmas: Outrageous Essays in Art & Art Education; Pun(k)Deconstruction: Experifigural Writings in Art & Art Education-, and Pedagogical Desire (forthcoming).

Political, Sociological, and Historical Background

Dec. 7, 1982: Eighteen years have passed since eighteen Latino students at Garfield High, located in LA's East Barrio, retook the Advanced Placement Test (APT) in calculus to exonerate themselves of cheating. Their teacher, Jaime Escalante, now 70 years old, became a legend as a result. In 1988 his story was immortalized on the screen with Stand and Deliver, starring Edward James Olmos as the 52-year-old balding Escalante, and a book, Escalante: The Best Teacher in America (Mathews) was published that same year. How are we as educators to understand this phenomenon of success? How are we to judge it? I remember distinctly how impressed I was when the film first came out. Escalante's innovative teaching techniques, I thought, were precisely what my undergraduate class in teacher education needed to understand. I thought they were generalizable to every situation. I even used excerpts of the film to highlight the ways a class might be won over.

Here I am, some twelve years later revisiting that memory. I read the book, The Best Teacher in America, for the very first time and reviewed the film once more. But this time I hated it! The radical disjunctures between the book, my now improved—although still limited—comprehension of the American political context at that time, and the fictional account of the movie read, to me, like a cover-up. If the film had lived up to the portrait in the book, the fraudulence of the phallus would have been exposed. Instead it remained veiled. For Ronald Reagan, of course, Escalante's success was a politician's dream come true. He called it the best movie he had ever seen, the epitome of what all teachers should and could do despite all the social and political obstacles stacked against them. Escalante was even called to the White House to shake his hand. I think now I know why.

Escalante's filmic narrative was the first inner-city high school movie released in North America since The Blackboard Jungle (1954), and has since been followed by a slew of similar “success” stories, such as, Lean on Me, based on yet another “true” story of Joe Clark, the principal of Paterson, New Jersey's inner-city school who took control of matters by using a bullhorn and a baseball bat, as well as other fictional accounts like Dangerous Minds, where, apparently, even a female teacher (LouAnne Johnson) was capable of similar heroic deeds, provided, of course, that she be an ex-U.S. Marine who could act tough and be versed in unarmed combat. Can a Lacanian psychoanalytic reading offer some insight as to what is going on in these, seemingly, extra-ordinary cases?

Žižek's Exemplary Culture

Dianne Chisholm

Dianne Chisholm

Dianne Chisholm   Professor of English at the University of Alberta. She is author of H.D.'s Freudian Poetics: Psychoanalysis in Translation (Cornell UP, 1992). Her nearly completed Queer Constellations: Fictions of Space in the Wake of the City uses Walter Benjamin's critical models of metropolitan modernity to read representations of social and sexual space in experimental narratives of late twentieth-century inner-city gay life. She is preparing to launch two related research projects: The Sublime Tragedy of Modern Mountaineering: Essays in the Ethics of the Real and Dissident Ascents: Women's Mountaineering in the Age of Feminism, or, Case Studies in a Subgenre of Subculture, 1955-1995.

Walter Benjamin commended as a theoretically productive and subversive procedure the reading of the highest spiritual products of a culture alongside its common, prosaic, worldly products. What he had in mind specifically was a reading of the sublime ideal of the love couple represented in Mozart's Magic Flute together with the definition of marriage found in Immanuel Kant (Mozart's contemporary), a definition that caused much indignation within moralistic circles. Marriage, Kant wrote, is “a contract between two adult persons of the opposite sex on the mutual use of their sex organs.” It is something of the same order that has been put to work in this book: a reading of the most sublime theoretical motifs of Jacques Lacan together with and through exemplary cases of contemporary mass culture: not only Alfred Hitchcock, about whom there is now some general agreement that he was, after all, a “serious artist,” but also film noir, science fiction, detective novels, sentimental kitsch, and up—or down—to Stephen King. … A kind of introduction to Lacanian “dogmatics” (in the theological sense of the term) … [this book] mercilessly exploits popular culture.

—Slavoj Žižek, “Preface” to Looking Awry

The logical result of Fascism is the introduction of aesthetics into political life. The violation of the masses, whom Fascism, with its Führer cult, forces to their knees, has its counterpart in the violation of an apparatus which is pressed into the production of ritual values.

—Walter Benjamin, “The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction”

What lessons are we, Žižek's faceless audience, to learn by reading Lacan's most sublime motifs “with and through exemplary cases of contemporary mass culture”? Does the author of Looking Awry (and innumerable other works that teach Lacan through kitsch readings of culture) not enjoin us, his implied novitiates, to cultivate an aesthetics of political life? His primer, after all, proceeds from Hitchcock and Stephen King to include such real horrors as the Chernobyl disaster, AIDS epidemics, and resurgent anti-Semitism. Does his procedure not trace a procession, “a whole series of ‘Lacan with …,’”1 that fills the empty, universal structure of subjectivation with a particular totality of homologous readings? Is this totalitarian procession not geared toward “the production of ritual values,” over which presides the Führer, the father, the discourse of the master, whose name is “Lacan”? Is this exemplification of Lacanian theory through mass trauma not reiterated, dogmatically and entertainingly, in a proselytising popular rhetoric that passes for a critique of ideology?

Daniel Rancour-Laferriere  

Dear Editor:

Recently I received the spring issue of JPCS (Vol. 6, No. 1), which contains David Bennett's article “Guilt as Capital: Psychoanalysis and the New Russians” (pp. 123-38). As a specialist in Russian culture and psychoanalysis, I read the article with great interest, but also with considerable dismay. The bulk of the article rehearses well-known facts about the history of psychoanalysis in Russia that are available in non-Russian sources (Bennett does not know Russian). The first few pages of the article, however, are outright defamatory.

Ideological Death and Grief in the Classroom: Mourning as a Prerequisite to Learning

Marshall Alcorn

Marshall Alcorn

Marshall Alcorn   Associate Professor of English and the Human Sciences at George Washington University. He is Executive Director for APCS and a Member of the Board of Directors for the Forum on Psychiatry and the Humanities. His books include Narcissism and the Literary Libido (NYUP, 1994) and Changing the Subject in English Class (SIUP, 2002).

In the last twenty years the character of writing instruction in English departments all over the country has changed dramatically. Basic assumptions about how writing should be taught have shifted from a paradigm that seeks to regulate correctness in writing to a paradigm that seeks to advance political progress in a body politic. Ten years ago, when this shift began to show clear momentum, there was considerable hope for at least one desirable consequence: that the power politics existing between student and teacher would disappear. Richard Boyd writes:

It was to be expected that the old narratives of instructor and student locked in a struggle of will would be replaced by a new version of a far more peaceable classroom where teachers might act more as collaborators than as adversaries. (590)

At least two thoughts supported this hope for a more peaceable classroom. First, the development of collaborative learning and writing made the teacher's position less central. He or she was no longer the single authority in matters of advice and evaluation. This was often experienced as liberating for both students and teachers. Second, however, the new theory itself offered a promise for easy change. New understandings of subjectivity argued that the self was not some category essential to human experience, but something imaginary. Because the self was not some real object, but an effect of language, it appeared something able to be easily shaped by language practices. Lacan's discussion of the mirror stage and Althusser's analysis of interpellation suggested to many that the powerful social forces that worked to construct subjectivity might also work in the classroom to reconstruct subjectivity. Many of us in the field of writing are trying to understand why this practice of working with human values, working with problems of ethics or politics in the classroom, is so difficult. The hope of happy students seeking personal and political understanding has been dampened by hard and painful experience. In the classroom it appears, as Boyd puts it, students seem “not wanting to participate in their own liberation” (591).

Some Remarks on the Symptom and the Social Link: Lacan with Marx

Alain Vanier

Alain Vanier

Alain Vanier   Practicing psychoanalyst and President of Espace Analytique, holds a license of letters in literature, a Ph.D. in clinical psychology, and an M.D. with a specialization in psychiatry. He teaches psychopathology and psychoanalysis at the University of Paris VII, where he is also Maitre de Conférences. One of his books, Lacan (The Lacanian Clinical Field) (2000), has recently been translated into English.

Although nothing predestined Lacan to come into contact with Marx, that encounter did take place early in his life through people and works influenced by Marxist theory. In the 1930s Lacan frequented the surrealist circle of poets, and between 1933 and 1938 he attended the lectures on Hegel given by Alexandre Kojève at the Ecole des Hautes Etudes. A more remote connection was Lacan's friendship with the Communist psychologist, Henri Wallon, for whom Lacan wrote Les complexes familiaux in 1938. Of course, the events of modern history also involved Lacan with Marx. Finally, it is well known how important Marxist thought was for the French intelligentsia of the postwar period.

Lacan stressed man's social being in his earliest writings, and he used Freud as a major reference, quoting, in particular, a passage from Group Psychology in which Freud notes how “in the individual's mental life someone else is invariably involved as a model, as an object, as a helper, as an opponent; and so, from the very first, individual psychology, in this extended but entirely justifiable use of the words, is at the same time social psychology as well” (69). The Other is thus involved with the subject from the beginning. In the same way, Lacan's stade du miroir—which he borrowed from Wallon and a number of other psychologists—demonstrates the necessity of an Other from which the subject can differentiate in order to build personal unity in the image. The “other” at that time was the subject's fellow man, his look-alike, but also the Other who names and whose mediation is needed to confer an image. For Henri Wallon, the premature birth generic to our species attested the biological roots of man's social being and explained the importance of imaginary capture. Indeed, the idea of premature birth allowed Lacan to theorize the anticipation of the maturation process evidenced in the stade du miroir, a concept which accounts for the importance of imaginary capture in man's life. We should note here that, at this stage in Lacan's writings, the subject's involvement with the group was mainly imaginary. Borrowing from Hegel's Master-Slave dialect, Lacan initially described desire as derived from the imaginary, and evidenced especially in jealousy. Desire, fundamentally alienated, is also the expression of the non-individuality of the subject. In addition, he observed that the paternal figure was in decline, although this figure was, for Freud, a necessary condition for there to be a group.

Writing as a Development in Interpersonal Relations

Charles Bazerman

Charles Bazerman

Charles Bazerman   Professor and Chair of Education at the University of California, Santa Barbara, has interests in the rhetoric of science and technology, writing across the curriculum, rhetorical theory, and the history of literacy. His most recent book, The Languages of Edison's Light, examines the rhetorical and representational work that made Edison's incandescent light a social reality. Previous books include Shaping Written Knowledge: The Genre and Activity of the Experimental Article in Science ; Constructing Experience-, Textual Dynamics of the Professions; Involved: Writing For College, Writing For Your Self and The Informed Writer: Using Sources in the Disciplines.

Language development is intensely imbricated with the development of one's social being, one's relations and cooperations with others, one's feelings of security and anxiety, one's full range of emotions, one's emotional connectedness and distances with others, and one's conscious view of oneself and others. Any adequate account of writing would see each of these issues at play in every text we write and read. Indeed, much literary interpretation examines such issues in a limited domain of texts where imagination is at free play. To understand these issues at work in other kinds of texts, it makes sense to look at the deep role of language in the formation of the self, which shapes the face one presents to the world and the inner self that seeks various forms of cooperation and relation to others. These issues are crucial for all writing education, because learning to write means learning to take on a bold presence in the world and enter into complex and sophisticated relations with others, whether one writes accountancy reports, ambassadorial greetings, journalistic accounts, or sociological studies. Students' development as writers is saturated with issues of identity, affect, elation, and one's place in the world.

A number of traditions have considered the relation of language development to the formation of social, communicative, active selves. Among those are the phenomenological tradition leading to microinteractional sociology (Heritage), the Soviet sociocultural tradition, which has spawned the more recent activity theory (Wertsch, Vygotsky, Luria, Cole, Engestrom), the eighteenth-century Scottish moralist and dissident traditions (Smith and Priestley, for examples), leading to the foundations of modern liberalism, and the American pragmatist tradition.

In the American pragmatist tradition, George Herbert Mead and John Dewey saw language development and social interaction as crucial in the formation of self, and they greatly influenced the founder of linguistic anthropology, Edward Sapir, who spent several years at Chicago with them. During those same years, at the recommendation of other Chicago sociologists, Sapir met the psychiatrist Harry Stack Sullivan, and they immediately became fast friends (Perry). Sullivan's contact with Sapir and the Chicago sociologists gave him the necessary concepts to fully develop his biographical approach to psychiatry, which he had been working on for the previous decade. The result was a psychiatrically rich account of the self, based in language and social development—an account which allows us to consider how writing builds upon deeply personal experiences of the self at the same time as it provides new spheres in which the self can develop in interaction with others (see also Bazerman).

The Sound of Sci(l)ence: Žižek's Concept of Ideology-Critique

Robert Resch

Robert Resch

Robert Resch   Teaches European intellectual history at Texas A&M University. He is the author of Althusser and the Renewal of Marxist Social Theory as well as several articles on contemporary politics and social theory.

This is the second of two articles on the social theory of Lacanian philosopher Slavoj Žižek. In its predecessor (Resch, “Empty”) I demonstrated that what I called the “Žižek effect in social theory,” namely Žižek's ability to generate seemingly profound yet maddeningly elusive interpretations of cultural phenomena, is created by violating the rules of logic, in particular, by combining subjective and objective, internal and external perspectives into an impossible unity. Žižek's obscurantism, I argued, emerges in the service of an ideological conception of the subject as emptiness, a fantasy of absolute Freedom that moves Žižek from a realist Lacanian theory of a concrete subject to a Lacanian mysticism of a sublime Subject. Based upon a mistaken identification of the Cartesian cogito and the Lacanian subject of the unconscious, Žižek's sublime Subject is posited as the antithesis of all determination. However, as I showed at some length, determinism is a demon that cannot be exorcised without slipping into irrationalism and incoherence.1

The present essay is a critique of Žižek's attempt, in “The Spectre of Ideology” (1994), to develop a concept of “ideology-critique” consistent with his fantasy of Freedom and the sublime Subject. In this well-known article, Žižek rejects all positive knowledge as indistinguishable from ideology and proposes to relocate the ground of ideology-critique in the immediate life experiences of the subject, specifically in experiences of social relations of domination. For Žižek, society is created on the basis of a traumatic antagonism that cannot be grasped or represented from within (without society itself disintegrating). Since all so-called social science (all positive knowledge of society) is structured on the basis of traumatic origins it cannot grasp, to believe that one possesses positive knowledge of society is an illusion; there is no way for positive knowledge to distinguish between ideology and science. However, the immediate experience of the subject is “non-ideological” insofar as “not all” of the subject is defined by existing relations of domination and their repressive systems of representation. The essence of the subject exists as a potentiality outside or beyond the symbolic order, an emptiness that undermines and opposes ideology and yet becomes ideological itself as soon as it is positively stated.

Gustavo Guerra

Gustavo Guerra

Gustavo Guerra   Assistant Professor of Humanities at Olivet College. His work has appeared, or will soon appear, in Style, Papers on Language and Literature, New Vico Studies, and Interdisciplinary Literary Studies. His current work centers on neopragmatism, psychoanalysis, and cultural theory. He is co-editing a book on the work of Slavoj Žižek.

For around ten years or so now, the work of the Slovenian philosopher Slavoj Žižek has become almost mandatory reading for anyone hoping to keep abreast of developments in the humanities in general. The breadth of his topics—ranging from an apparently straightforward explication of basic psychoanalytic concepts, to the nature of political oppression, to the relationship between Marxism and Christianity—is sure to address the concerns of various, even differing, intellectual constituencies. And it should not be surprising that the group of scholars who identify their own work as “theoretical” should be quickly drawn to such interdisciplinary work. But the immediate appeal Žižek has had among Americanists seems particularly anomalous. Aside from the fact that some of his books are originally written in English, and that he unquestionably has a major investment in American popular culture, there is nothing in his works that should be particularly appealing to an American critical or philosophic mentality. Tom Cohen, for instance, has logically argued that given the pragmatist bent that has reigned in the American philosophic tradition, Žižek's thought may be hard put to appeal to the interest of those operating within that frame of mind. Drenched as it is in Hegelian, Lacanian, and post-foundational Marxist philosophy, the Žižekian discourse is precisely what pragmatist thinkers strive to avoid, if not plainly ignore. Similarly, Denise Gigante characterizes Žižek's work as an attempt to reconstruct the concept of “ideology” from a Kantian perspective.1 In placing Žižek within a Kantian reflective framework, Gigante removes Žižek even further from any apparent relationship to American philosophy. Thus it is even harder to address my initial curiosity about why Žižek has become so popular within the Americanist discourse; but it is still harder, in fact, to address why one should even care in the first place. Why not simply yield to the temptation of dismissing his work as the latest, passing, fancy in academia these days? I argue that to understand his work as pragmatist is a refusal to discuss him in those tempting but simplistically naive terms; it is, moreover, to reveal a particularly compelling use of his work: insofar as pragmatism's primary aim is to achieve a better society, I will argue that Žižek's pragmatic oeuvre has the same lofty aim.

In a lovely chapter of his book Einstein's Dreams, Alan Lightman explores our ail-too human experiences and constructs of time. “In this world,” Lightman writes, “there are two times. There is mechanical time and there is body time. The first is as rigid and metallic as a massive pendulum of iron that swings back and forth, back and forth, back and forth. The second squirms and wriggles like a bluefish in a bay. The first is unyielding, predetermined. The second makes up its mind as it goes along.”1 It is the issue of time that I'd like to address. Of time and the times we inhabit, and about the peculiar relationship that psychoanalysts, in particular, have to time and history. A question arises immediately: mechanical time, or time of the body? In the writer's words: “For miraculously, a barrister, a nurse, a baker can make a world in either time, but not in both times.” I'm sure that Einstein, who in the fertility of his delirium played with the concept as ruthlessly as anyone, would say the same holds true for a psychoanalyst. “Each time is true, but the truths are not the same,” writes Lightman. Perhaps especially for a psychoanalyst. Another man, from another time and context but of equal stature to Einstein, put forth something of the same idea. His argument was that we ought not to serve two masters, indeed, that the very proposition is untenable. Which brings me to an incident that occurred several years ago, at the clinical facility of my psychoanalytic training institute.

I happened to walk in one afternoon on a group of trainees who were engaged, albeit in a kind of lazy and listeless way, in a conversation whose overtones escaped me. I'd remained on the fringes of the conversation until a second-year student approached and drew me into the friendly fray. Apparently, the young man had been polling his peers on the attractiveness and feasibility of various graduate degree options, when, with the respect due a slightly senior colleague, he asked me what I'd studied in college. “Italian, and then anthropology,” I answered. I sensed what was coming.

Introduction

In the aftermath of the conflict in the Balkans and in particular the latest pogrom in Kosovo, social scientists are starting to try to make some sense of the atrocities and human rights violations that have taken place there. This paper relays some first impressions from a recent visit to Pristina in the heart of Kosovo earlier in the year. We suggest some ways in which we might start thinking psychoanalytically about the current conditions in which the population of Kosovo live. This piece is too short to attempt an extensive analysis, but it is intended to give the reader a first-hand taste of some of the experiences that were encountered during this research. We start by outlining some of the basic feelings that the observer encounters when first in Kosovo, before going on to discuss some of the psycho-dynamics at work in the interplay between Serbian and Albanian residents. Finally, we suggest that some of the key dynamics that were at the heart of the eruption of ethnic hatred in Kosovo are currently part of the strategy for peace keeping. We question the viability of this in terms of both finding a solution for conflict and re-building Kosovo, and we ask how we are to move from a position of splitting difference to a point of the reconciliation of difference.

First Impressions

The first impressions of Pristina were not quite what one would expect. A year had passed since the end of the NATO bombing campaign against Serbian forces in Kosovo. One might have expected to see large-scale physical damage and destruction and an air of sobriety. The opposite, however, seemed to be the case. Buildings were largely intact, and one was greeted by a mood of jubilation as people celebrated their freedom from Serbian oppression.

The idea behind this book—to commission and reprint a set of essays devoted to Freud's comparatively neglected study “The Psychogenesis of a Case of Homosexuality in a Woman”—was an excellent one. The result—a rich blend of contemporary U.S. feminism, self-identified postmodernism, queer theory, and predominantly relational psychoanalysis, all hastily printed and bound by Routledge—is as much a product of its historical moment as was Freud's wildly incoherent 1920 case. While the book thoroughly illuminates social, psychical, and cultural forces informing Freud's haute-bourgeois Viennese milieu, it also sheds a revealing light on the psychoanalytic world of 1990s New York.

That Obscure Subject of Desire is structured dialogically as a series of responses to Freud's case, which the editors sensibly include at the start of the book. After “Psychogenesis” come five essays by academics, most notably Teresa de Lauretis, followed by seven pieces by New York clinicians, with a substantial afterword by supervising analyst Muriel Dimen. Dimen accomplishes some of the work that the book's introduction might have performed by sketching an overview of relational psychoanalysis—a “polyglot” theoretical orientation that combines object-relations psychoanalysis (especially Winnicott) with the self-psychology of Kohut and the interpersonal tradition of Harry Stack Sullivan—which academic readers largely unfamiliar with this contemporary clinical development will find helpful. Dimen's essay is couched as a response to the contributors' responses to Freud, and is preceded by editor Erica Schoenberg's chapter, the book's penultimate piece, which also responds to many of the collection's arguments and insights.

Divided between academics and clinicians, the book seems to want to stage a dialogue between disciplines, but I am not sure that it succeeds. The selection of contributors is weighted toward clinicians; when you include Freud, the ratio of analysts to academics is 2:1. All the clinicians (except, of course, Freud) are associated with New York University's postdoctoral program in psychotherapy and psychoanalysis—a very interesting institutional space, to be sure, but not quite the hotbed of intellectual diversity that it sometimes imagines itself to be. Apart from de Lauretis, our foremost theorist of lesbian desire, all the academic contributors are also based in New York. Dialogue among this social set is fascinating and lively, although the voices involved often sound remarkably alike from any vantage outside Manhattan.

Is psychoanalysis always antithetical to the cultural study of race? With its emphasis on desire, the discourses of le grand Autre, and the méconnaissances of identity, psychoanalytic criticism would appear to be a rather unproductive model for historicist scholars who study particularized minority subject-positions. Indeed, many African-American critics have frequently exhibited a knee-jerk reaction once scholars attempt to apply the writings of Freud, Lacan, or Klein to black texts. And when a black critic utilizes psychoanalytic models for textual interpretation, the critical response can become even more acute. As Claudia Tate asked herself after one scholar of African-American literature skeptically derided her project, “Didn't I know that psychoanalysis is inappropriate and perhaps even detrimental to black agency?” (16). Her carefully crafted Psychoanalysis and Black Novels, however, radically departs from traditional black scholarship by writing against the standard modes of interpretation and canon-formation upheld by many African-American critics.

African-American critics, Tate notes in her introduction, often urge that the black literary text promotes social change; the black novel, they insist, must function as a public protest that both uplifts the race and troubles the pernicious social institutions that govern (and constrain) black agency. Psychoanalysis and Black Novels begins by querying this fetishization of “agency,” arguing that critics of the black novel must acknowledge the oftentimes destabilizing operations of desire—the metonymic and metaphoric signifiers of the unconscious—that also play a significant role in the construction of textual meaning and black subjectivity. In so doing, Tate shifts her critical lens away from the cultural production of race and concentrates instead on the exigencies of the psyche, the private wishes and personal desires of black authors and their literary creations. To be even more precise, Tate places the protocols of race and the operations of desire in an uneasy dialogue. Reading the black novel through the lens of psychoanalysis, her book asks: How does intrapsychic longing disrupt intersubjective minority collectivities? What role does perverse pleasure play in the material production of black identity? And what can non-canonical works tell us about the fantasmatic agendas of canonized black authors as well as African-American literary canon formation?

Robert Samuels

Robert Samuels

Many of the articles in this issue come from the APCS conference on “Education and the Unconscious” held at the University of California, Santa Barbara in November 2000. Throughout the conference, many of the participants continued to return to the question of what psychoanalysis can tell us about the fundamental relations between teachers and students. This special issue on Psychoanalysis and Education helps to address this question by examining such topics as the role of death, mourning, and anxiety in the learning process; the problems of student resistances and teacher burn-out; the conflict between the personal and the social in psychoanalysis and education; the unconscious aspects of the teaching relationship; and the effect of new technologies on the teaching of writing and other academic subjects.

Instead of outlining and paraphrasing these important essays, I want to focus on the psychopathology of everyday academic life. While my examination will be centered on the field of English Studies, I believe that my analysis and conclusions are valid for most areas of higher education.

Narcissism and the Teaching of English

My central hypothesis is that most English departments are dominated by a group structure shaped by many of the main features of a narcissistic personality disorder: a pervasive pattern of grandiosity (in fantasy or behavior), a strong need for admiration, and lack of empathy (DSM-IV). My goal here is not to label people or to call people names, especially since I am a member of this group; rather, I want to explore a shared psychology and offer some possible advice for intervention strategies.

The narcissistic personality structure is one of the most difficult to change because of an intense underlying sense of vulnerability and an equally intense system of defenses. In order to fully grasp this structure, one must realize that the paradoxical nature of narcissism is defined by a simultaneous coupling of grandiosity with an unconscious sense of subjective nothingness. Since a narcissist defines him- or herself in a mirroring or idealizing relation with an Other, any lack of recognition by the Other leads to a complete sense of worthlessness.

Problems in Communicative Language Teaching in Korea

Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) has emphasized more personal, interactive, “functional” and “social” aspects of language use “in real situations and real time” (Littlewood xi; 1-7).2 With the advent of CLT, EFL learners need to develop skills in “processing” social and situational factors beyond fixed linguistic forms, “selecting” acceptable language forms, and finally “using” them for communicating meanings as efficiently as possible (see Reivers; Littlewood 4, 89). To this end, EFL learners are also to be empowered to “freely” create meanings with the English language they have learned, which they want to convey to others, while doing “creative play with patterns of meaning” (Carter, Investigating 158—63) in “free, spontaneous interaction” (Savignon 24). However, CLT in Korea has to date remained at the level of what Rinvolucri calls “semi-communicative” exercises in which learners merely do “rehearsal activities” with a piece of prepackaged text of “psychologically contentless information” “in a mood of relative communicative apathy” (195-96). This is because most EFL practitioners and specialists in Korea have mistaken communication for “information transfer” such as ordering food, asking for directions, taking messages, buying items, describing places (or people/things), giving information about objects, and so on. Here, communicating in English is far from “interactive activities that depend on varying types of relationships with others”—the relationships which involve “more personal aspects of one's being, such as feelings” (Arnold and Brown 8—9):

Indeed, the most fascinating subject we can learn about and talk about is ourselves. And we learn about ourselves through others. So communication which satisfies these deep, innate needs develops from sharing about ourselves while others actively listen to us, showing understanding and accepting us as we are. (Moskowitz 178; emphasis in the original).

Still worse, to memorize dialogues that are “transparent and transactional and devoid of richness, cultural reference and creativity is to misrepresent what speakers actually do” (Carter, Investigating 166): “It is possible for the student to perform these tasks without ever being exposed to extended discourse or discussions conducted at a level of abstraction that is removed from the listener/reader” (Swaffar et al. 2). Since those dialogues are fixed and predictable, and further because the EFL listener is in a mood of communicational apathy, these task-oriented communicative exercises are “dummy runs” in that “energetic, motivated exchange of real, personal information” never takes place (Rinvolucri 197).

He is currently preparing for a sabbatical leave from his teaching duties at Red Deer College to pursue work on the images of masculinity emerging from the work of Canadian prairie novelists.

Introduction

Mathew Coon Come is Grand Chief of the Assembly of First Nations in Canada. He is also a Cree from Northern Quebec who, as a child, was sent by the Canadian federal government to a residential school run by the Catholic Church. The residential schools in Canada, run by both Catholic and Protestant churches, took native children from their local communities and attempted to strip them of their culture, language, and spirituality, in order to eventually assimilate them into the mainstream of Canadian society. At the residential schools the practice of the cut was initiated: to cut Aboriginal children off from their cultural heritage: their language, dress, and “pagan” beliefs. Coon Come himself experienced this as traumatic.

In response to the claims for redress concerning these historical practices (the residential schools are no longer operative; the last ones closed down in the early 1970s), the federal government, and the mainline churches who ran the schools, have agreed to a monetary liability and also have issued a formal apology to the victims of the residential schools and their families.

Mathew Coon Come, speaking for the Assembly of First Nations, has rejected this apology, and has called for a Truth and Reconciliation Commission, similar to the one initiated in South Africa, maintaining that much more work of mourning and love needs to take place between non-Aboriginal Canadians and Aboriginal Canadians in order to bring about reconciliation (Dueck 2000).

It is interesting to note that Mathew Coon Come is a devout Catholic Christian, and an overwhelming majority of First Nations people identify themselves as Christian, both Protestant and Catholic (Dueck 2000). This is important to note because the conflict over the residential schools is not a conflict between non-Aboriginal Christians and Aboriginal non-Christians, but involves a call for love and reconciliation that is in keeping with a long history in the land called Canada, going back to the first explorers, that is both Aboriginal and Christian.

Nick Tingle

Nick Tingle

Nick Tingle   Works in the UCSB Writing Program and currently is writing a book provisionally titled, “Self-Knowledge: Writing Pedagogy and Psychoanalysis.”

As a long-time teacher of academic writing, I can testify that beginning students do not understand academic theory, graduating students still have not mastered it, and the take-home lesson for most, on the basis of their university experience, is that an “academic question” is synonymous with a useless or pointless question. That such is the case does not seem to me the result of some lack in students' genetic make-up, in their gray matter, or in their cognitive capacities. Rather, I think the movement into academic theory entails on the part of the individual a difficult and sometimes painful psychological movement, one for which Hegel's phrase, the labor of the negative, is not entirely inappropriate.

I describe the psychological dimension of this labor of the negative through reference to self-psychology. Briefly and in the grossest term, self-psychological theory holds that individuals seek, in the world, objects (specifically selfobjects) that mirror and empathetically affirm their narcissistically informed and energized ideals and ambitions. If individuals are able to locate such objects, then they experience themselves as ongoing continuous wholes and as independent centers of initiative. If individuals, however, are unable to locate such objects, they may experience self-fragmentation with such attendant affects as anxiety, depression, and rage.

This is my premise: the movement into theory may require of students that they experience a degree of self-fragmentation or narcissistic wounding. In my work as a teacher of writing, I have come to recognize three broad categories of such wounding. These I will detail here. In fact, of course, these three responses are inter-related, and all three may indeed occur in any given student over the course of his development or in response to a single assignment. Roughly, these three responses may be described as (a) the rageful, (b) the listless or de-energized, and (c) as the anxious.

The rageful is perhaps the most obvious. This is the response of the student who experiences the encounter with a theory, whatever it might be, as directly contradicting a belief or throwing it into question. The student is relatively conscious of the belief and holds it rather rigidly. One student for example, in response to an assignment on Freud's article on infantile sexuality, decorated the cover page of his paper with a cartoon, depicting an infant, with little devil horns protruding from its head, sitting on its potty and sucking its thumb. The caption read: “I want to suck my mother.” The cartoon was quite well done.

Patrick McHugh

Patrick McHugh

Patrick McHugh   Currently teaches in the Writing Program at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Resistance is futile. You will be assimilated.

—Borg Credo from Star Trek

Students do not live by reason alone, not even in composition classes; nor do teachers live by reason alone, not even in composition classes. Yet most if not all composition teachers, theorists,

305

and administrators agree, quite rightly, that the most important task of first-year writing courses at American colleges and universities is to engage students in critical thinking. The course functions as an introduction to the discourses of reason, their reflective distance, their rules of presentation and disputation, their demands for rigorous form and precise language. Since all students with few exceptions typically take the course, it is the gatekeeper class for competency in the rational use of language. In other words, reason is the lingua franca of adult, professional, public life. Each of us defines or discovers who we are in part within the “space” opened by that language. Composition students are often just beginning this process of self-definition/self-discovery, or at least beginning at a new, higher level of maturity and expectation.

Yet students do not live by reason alone. Their experience in composition typically involves what I will call here the “affect of reason,” which is to say a whole complex of often unreasonable emotions. This is not even counting the emotions associated with leaving home, discovering themselves, and emerging from adolescent fog, in the context of which composition class is barely a blip on the emotional screen. Yet as anyone who has taught—or taken—composition knows, students also respond specifically to the discourses of reason, and they respond emotionally. They feel confused, or insecure, or confident; they are indifferent, or disdainful, or surprised; they show fear or determination, sometimes anger or pride, sometimes even joy and wonder. Moreover, at stake in their engagement with reason is not simply their competency, their grade, their academic career. If we are successful as teachers, students might get beyond what philosophers call “instrumental reason,” beyond the problem-solving skills they will use on the job, and start to see the intrinsic value of rational discourse. They might engage what philosophers call free or “pure” reason or what we usually mean by “critical thinking,” which leads to an understanding of the world and one's place and one's role in it. In these cases, at stake for students in composition classes is their identity, their way of being in the world.

Higher Education's (Mis)appropriations of Therapeutic Discourse

Janet Thormann

Janet Thormann

Janet Thormann   Teaches English composition and literature at the College of Marin, Kentfield, California, and psychoanalytic theory at the Lacanian School of Psychoanalysis in Berkeley. She is on the editorial board and a contributor to Literature and Psychology and the Journal of European Psychoanalysis and edits ANa MORPHOSIS. The system of education is today in the United States one of the primary means through which power forms compliant citizens who conform to state power. Like many other contemporary social networks and institutions—religion, the penal system, political commentary, the entertainment industry—institutions of education adapt to their own purposes a popularized discourse of therapy and psychological individualism that dilutes psychoanalytic theory and practice. Such psychologism is not only a simplistic dilution of the complexities of psychoanalysis; by enlisting psychoanalysis to naturalize a soothing cultural ideology, the psychologizing discourse of power perverts psychoanalysis's capacities for oppositional analysis and ethical action. Lacan's consistent objections to forms of American ego psychology and object relations therapies are, I think, expressions of the obstinate resistance of psychoanalysis to its use by modern state formations.

The discourse of therapeutic culture is especially apparent in higher education in California—that is, in the community college and state college and university systems, as well as in private colleges and universities. I want here to look at the prevalence of that discourse in a number of symptomatic locations: in the discourse of the profession, in admissions policy that has succeeded affirmative action in the University of California system, and in UC Berkeley's multiculturalism requirement.

First, influenced by counseling departments and administrative bureaucracies, instructors adopt a vocabulary of therapeutic psychology to describe and direct what they do in the classroom. So, for example, the purpose of higher education is said to be “raising self-esteem.” Teachers are reluctant to “assert authority” by grading student work and hence use methods of “peer evaluation” whereby students grade each other's work and provide their own final grades. Or, since extensive commentary on student writing is said to “inhibit confidence,” “organic” or “holistic” reading is practiced, whereby only a portion of an entire paper receives a reader's attention. Grading generally is discouraged as “punitive”: the University of California at Santa Cruz only this past November reintroduced a grading system in place of a system of teachers' letters of evaluation that itself was substituted for grading, and Stanford University two years ago reintroduced failing grades in its classes. Such a general refusal of professional judgment, exemplified by an unwillingness to critique or grade is said to “empower learning.

Diane O'Donoghue

Diane O'Donoghue   Holds faculty appointments in the Department of Visual and Critical Studies at Tufts University/School of the Museum of Fine Arts and at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, where she has been an affiliated member since 1998. An art historian, her work in the psychoanalytic context examines Freud's constructions of visuality, especially as they informed the production of location, desire, and “antiquity.” She will be the Fulbright/Sigmund Freud Visiting Scholar in Psychoanalysis at the University Vienna for 2001-2002.

My pedagogic experiences within a psychoanalytic institute often resonate with those of my academic life; one must struggle in both sites to respect and resist students' expectation of an arrival at definitive “knowledge.” However, examining Freud's texts with analytic candidates seemed to throw this moment-to-moment negotiation into particularly sharp relief. More so than usual, I find myself deeply concerned with the potential for reinscription, because it seems especially difficult to avoid perpetuating certain discursive constructions, even in the context of their critique. In some cases, such as with writings concerning “hysteria,” it proved useful to examine how the reiteration of the very word itself creates the productive site of its meaning-making, and from this can develop other discussions of the totalizing functions of naming, in psychoanalysis and elsewhere. These same issues can certainly also be said for the evocation of “Oedipus” and its role in the framing of normative heterosexuality. I would like to continue with the oedipal construction in this essay and to make use of it to initiate another site of inquiry. Upon this well-trodden path of Freud's thematics of sexuality, I will attempt to overlay an additional mode of passage. In a strategy that might appear to join disparate narratives, Freud's configurations of infantile sexuality will be located here within his childhood experiences of migration. This turn opens a pedagogic space where future analysts can examine information that has traditionally been considered in excess of the enframement of “oedipal” meaning. The resulting discussion affords the opportunity to consider how such exclusions create and maintain canonical readings and what the implications are of such foreclosures upon clinical practice.

This is arguably an ambitious undertaking, and one that will be limited here to the examination of an early memory that Freud offered as evidence of the “awakening” of desire for his mother. This recollection, occurring only days before his initial suggestion of a universalized childhood drama that would bear the name “Oedipus,” has intractably melded his memory to the subsequent paradigm. I would like to relocate this “awakening” and situate it instead within the moment—and the place—in which it supposedly occurred: on a train that carried members of the Freud family across a portion of central Europe between 1859 and 1860. In my reading, because desire cannot be splintered from dislocation, they will be posited here as coproductive; at the moment of this memory, the nascent “oedipal complex” was, following a phrase from Homi Bhabha, “neither the one nor the other” (25). In putting the oedipal construction quite literally on track, inquiries open that would otherwise be repeatedly obscured. This may suggest some future places of potentially fruitful investigation, among them the possibility that, for Freud, the “attainment” of heterosexuality may have been informed and valorized by his experiences of arriving at a specific destination.

Edward Gamarra

Edward Gamarra

Edward Gamarra   2000-2001 Fellow of the American Psychoanalytic Association, received a B.A. in Psychology from Vassar College and an M.A. in Cinema Studies from NYU. Currently he is ABD at Emory University's Graduate Institute of the Liberal Arts, where he is writing a dissertation on comedy and perversion. His other articles cover topics ranging from cultural pathology to postmodernism, from the horror genre to Gen X sexuality. He is actively involved in the American Psychoanalytic Association's Ad Hoc Committee on Psychoanalytic Studies Programs.

In the previous issue of JPCS, I examined how English-language scholarship on German humor has typically stressed the social and political elements of films and the corporate-governmental film industry production process. The preoccupation with the Ufa studio is just one way American scholars have perpetuated the notion that German visual arts were geared solely toward propaganda. I wanted to foreground the role ethnic prejudice has played in limiting scholarly inquiry into a neglected area. This second installment incorporates firsthand observations and interviews with native Germans to demonstrate what Germans have to say on the matter of their national character and supposed lack of humor. Before leaving for Berlin and Munich my central intellectual concern was to find how the American tendency to refuse Germans any capacity for humor influenced German self-perception. The secondary problem was how that which American popular culture associates with German identity—order, bureaucracy, anality—actually played out in Germany. In June of 1998, I left for Berlin and Munich. My field work began on the plane as I read the popular brand of Let's Go travel books, which observed, “There are, to be sure, certain German traits—industriousness, efficiency, and a mystifying refusal to cross the street against the light—but the generation of Germans who came of age after the war defy the negative stereotype of the humorless, heel-clicking German authoritarian” (59). I could not help but think of Freud's story of the borrowed kettle. Upon returning the pot to its owner, the neighbor is told there is a dent in the pot. The neighbor replies, “I didn't dent the pot,” adds, “The pot was already dented when I borrowed it,” and leaves saying, “I didn't borrow the pot anyway.” Similarly, multiple layers of denial permeate our understanding of German comedy. In our case, we might say, “Americans don't find German films to be funny, and so, at least to Americans, there are no German comedies”; “Germans can't make comedies that are funny even to Germans, and so there are no German comedies”; and “Germans are just not a funny people, and so there are no German comedies.” The end result is the same no matter how the situation is reformulated. Once in Berlin, I learned just how important comedy is to contemporary German culture.

“What does Lacan have to do with the political?” Feminist theory has long debated the political implications of Lacan's work, and post-structuralism its implications for politics. However, Anglophone political and social theory generally has been resistant to Lacanian psychoanalysis, characterizing it as irrelevant to political issues or dismissing it as “psychoanalysis.” Lacan and the Political presents a cogent and compelling argument for rethinking the importance of Lacan's work for contemporary political theory. This book shows how Lacanian psychoanalysis reconfigures our understanding of the political. It examines how the Lacanian theory of the real, the symbolic, and the imaginary provides a radically new conception of the political field. Rather than conceiving politics as the operation of given institutions and structures, the book argues that symbolic and fantasmic relations constitute the political field.

In this way, Lacan and the Political highlights the importance of the psychoanalytic problematic for political theory. The challenge of Lacanian psychoanalysis to existing concepts of the political lies in its insistence that imaginary and symbolic relations constitute political relations, and hence that the political field is necessarily incomplete. Traditional political theory examines the position of the conscious willing political agent and the institutions created by that agent. By contrast, a psychoanalytic political theory emphasizes the production of the affective and unconscious subject in the representational and fantasmic field of the political. Lacan and the Political engages with the task of developing such a psychoanalytic political theory. It shows how Lacan's theories have been crucial to rethinking the political in the work of Ernesto Laclau, Chantai Moufife, and Slavoj Žižek. It sets out the Lacanian foundations of these reconceptions of the political, thereby articulating the specificity of Lacanian political theory. In this way, Lacan and the Political presents an important articulation and development of Lacanian political theory. The book shows the relation between Lacan's work and the development of this new form of political theory in three crucial stages: first, it delineates the conceptual elements of Lacanian thought which are important for political theory; second, it shows how Lacan's ideas reconfigure our understanding of the political; and third, it develops a Lacanian theory of the political in relation to “traditional fantasmic politics” and radical democracy.
