Trauma and the Conservation of African-American Racial Identity

Sheldon George

Sheldon George

Sheldon George   Fourth-year Ph.D. student in the Department of English at Boston College. His work focuses on African-American literature and psychoanalytic and race theory. Race and slavery are central focuses in the courses he teaches at Boston College, which include a freshman writing seminar that models personal narratives after slave narratives, an elective on the novels of Toni Morrison and a core American literature course entitled “Tradition and Counter-Tradition.”

W.E.B. Du Bois asserts in “The Conservation of Races” that to achieve social equality African-Americans must conserve the concept of race and maintain their “race identity” (“Conservation” 248). Many African-Americans today support Du Bois's position, claiming that they maintain the concept of race as a means to fight politically against racism. African-American critic Lucius Outlaw, for example, argues that because of “continuing legacies of invidious ethnocentrism and racism” in America, justice cannot be “achieved without consideration of race and ethnicity” (18). However, Anthony Appiah's critique of Du Bois in his essay “Illusions of Race” implies that it is not only the political utility of race that causes African-Americans to use and conserve this concept; often, it is also an unconditional attachment to the concept of race itself. Appiah reveals that whether or not Du Bois was able to use the concept of race to escape “racism, [Du Bois] never completed the escape from race” itself (45). But Appiah cannot identify the agency that produces in African-Americans like Du Bois this attachment to race. How do we explain this attachment to race that goes beyond race's political utility?

I propose that the conservation of race by African-Americans often masks an effort to conserve the trauma of a racial history. Here, in keeping with Jacques Lacan's description of trauma as a “form” of the real, I will view slavery as an intrusive traumatic past, a real with which African-Americans maintain a psychological link through race (Fundamental 55). African-American racial identity functions to both maintain the traumatic real as a center of the self and to exclude the real from consciousness. The allegiance African-Americans feel toward the concept of race does not stem only from race's ability to protect them from what Outlaw calls the “legacies of racism.” It stems also from race's ability to establish for them a link with the trauma of slavery, while simultaneously offering itself as protection from a conscious encounter with this trauma.

“There are two, and only two, sexes!” asserts defiantly, and very much against the grain of postmodern Anglo-American gender theory, this new, thoroughly wide-ranging but uneven volume on the Lacanian theory of sexuation and its cultural, political, and ethical consequences. A warning, however: Before jumping to the over-hasty conclusion that this declaration subtends reactionary, homophobic, and both theoretically and scientifically naive assumptions about either the “nature” or “social construction” of human sexuality, it would be wise to pause for a moment to appreciate what exactly these Lacanians are trying to get across with their notion of “sexuation,” and to realize that, in order to understand this idea on its own terms, much of what contemporary feminist and queer theories now routinely take for granted—more specifically, their conceptual reliance on social constructionism as well as the related sex and gender binary and the cultural “deconstruction” of gender—must be held up to further analytic scrutiny.

As is undoubtedly already quite apparent, I find myself to a very large extent sympathetic to what this anthology, very polemically, one might add, attempts to assert. Nevertheless, I find it necessary, before delving into the anthology itself, to express two reservations. First, though ethically admirable and undoubtedly politically necessary to a significant degree, the strategy of the Lacanian collective to circumscribe its discussion of sexuation within the exclusive domain of Lacanian theory itself has the danger of perpetuating the misunderstandings that have plagued the Anglo-American reception of Lacan, particularly in feminist and antihomophobic circles. Now the alternative, in my view, is not a politically correct form of “dialogue” between antagonistic theoretical camps. What remains possible, nonetheless, is a thoroughgoing analysis of the differing assumptions that structure the Lacanian and deconstructionist-culturalist views of sex and sexuality, and I hope to accomplish (somewhat) modestly some of that in what follows. And second, be forewarned, gentle reader, that my appraisal of this anthology's work will not be without a hysterical component, and that I will want to decry what we might very loosely, and without much theoretical rigor, call the “lack of homosexual knowledge” in the Lacanian Other.

Anomie

In his monumental study on suicide, Emile Durkheim coined the term “anomie” to describe societies in which norms are unclear, contradictory, or unsuitable to the circumstances of their time. Durkheim focused on the implications that anomie has on the collective, proposing that it might result in anarchy or in the disintegration of the social structure. He argued that societies are obliged to construct a framework to restrict human aspirations to levels which can be attained given the limitations on resources, but that where this framework breaks down, these human aspirations would know no bounds and that the resulting despair would lead to a rise in the incidence of suicide.

Durkheim's concept of anomie was subsequently developed by Merton to provide a generalized theory of deviant behavior. Merton focused in particular on the condition in which a society provided clear enough guidance concerning which goals were socially approved, but gave a relatively little attention to the means by which these goals should be reached. The consequence of this, Merton argued, was that individuals would be minded to use illegitimate means to gain socially approved goals (Adler and Laufer). According to Merton, this phenomenon could be witnessed in relation to one of the core Americans goals, the pursuit of entrepreneurial success: despite the belief embodied in the constitution of the United States that all Americans are created equal, it was evident that the social structure did not provide equal opportunities for all groups. Thus, lower socio-economic groups and various immigrants and ethnic minorities found themselves at a disadvantage in pursuit of the fruits of economic success. In this situation many, perhaps most, of those so disadvantaged came to terms with the circumstances in which they found themselves, but some of them could not accept matters as they are and adopted a variety of responses—innovation, ritualism, retreatism, rebellion, crime—all of which have in common a refusal to conform to the prevailing view of what are acceptable means to achieve socially approved goals. By the responses just described, individuals and groups seek to close or bridge the gap between widely endorsed opportunities.

Dear Editor:

Yesterday I received and read with great surprise something like a detective story—almost a horror story—about myself; about the East-European Institute of Psychoanalysis, which is headed by me; and about the current state of psychoanalysis in Russia as a whole. What I am referring to is David Bennett's article “Guilt as Capital: Psychoanalysis and the New Russians,” which was published in the journal you edit (Vol. 6, No. 1, Spring 2001, under “International Notes,” pp. 123-38).

Permit me to make the following comments:

(1) p. 123: The author refers to a “houseboat,” and then on p. 124 refers to “multi-story houseboat,” and “preferred operational bases of eastern European Mafia.”

In fact, the boat in question is an ordinary river barge (without an engine), with living quarters. This barge, which had been standing idle for several years at the entrance of the city park, was bought from the government at closeout prices by the husband of one of my students. Afterwards, a sort of country house was built onto it, which also serves (and continues to serve to this day) as a gallery of contemporary art. The houseboat is now in fact quite beautiful and is designed for comfort and convenience. In it there are indeed several guest bedrooms. As for the mirror on the ceiling, this is only a figment of the rich imagination of the author.

My student's husband has no connection whatsoever with the Mafia. He is a very successful businessman, in some sense a financial genius, and a great admirer of art. Last year he financed yet another gallery of contemporary Saint Petersburg art, located downtown in the Nevsky Prospekt area.

For ethical reasons I cannot go into details, but I can say that the wife of this businessman, after successfully finishing our Institute, perhaps for the first time found her place in life. At present she is a well-known art critic in the city. Because of these facts, the husband of my former student has a special respect for our Institute. He is also a great admirer of America. For him to invite the Conference participants to his private houseboat residence on July 4th, American Independence Day, was his way of expressing respect for America, and was also a demonstration of his respect for the Institute.

From the perspective of psychoanalytic self psychology, a healthy individual engages the world with exploration, self-assertion, vitality, and reciprocity, to creatively, and productively, nourish sense of self, other, and community. The relation between the experiences of exploration, self-assertion, vitality, and reciprocity, and the ability to be productive, holds many keys to understanding creativity, why it mystifies us, and why it is valued by society. One's vitality is nourished and supported by exploration and self-assertion, for to be vital is not just to be authentic to self, but to feel a direct connection between one's subjective sense of self and one's actions into the world. Through action one feels the exhilaration of truly being alive, of finding competency and meaning, of feeling that one's intersection with the world sustains, and develops, one's nature. At the same time, this intersection is dynamic and one's vitality is reinforced and expanded by the mutual influence of one's environment. Productivity demonstrates this reciprocal exchange between sense of self and one's surrounding world.

Through such experiences individuals find people, places, things, ideas, and activities that serve what self psychologists call “selfobject functions”—psychological support systems that enhance an experience of self as whole and cohesive. Prevalent throughout our lives, these selfobject functions change and adapt to our psychic progression. In health the young selfobject needs of the child transform into the more mature selfobject needs of the adult. In art-making, the medium of the art form serves vital selfobject functions, deeply influencing the creative process. Throughout life creativity involves exploration and self-assertion, through a multi-leveled subjective relationship that serves significant selfobject functions through the construction of an ideal form that embodies and expands self-delineation, self-cohesion, and self-development, and that is ultimately self-transformative.

The strange behaviour of patients, in being able to combine a conscious knowing with not knowing, remains inexplicable by what is called normal psychology.

—Freud, SE 12: 142

However different the Freud biographies may be, they are unanimous on one point: Freud wanted to know. From the outset, we see an ambitious man at work whose goal is to reach a Master position through knowledge. When he takes his first steps toward psychoanalysis—he is at that stage middle-aged—his goal is still the same, and this colors both his initial theory and his practice. The analytic cure is a search for lost knowledge, lost as a result of its becoming unconscious; the aim of the treatment is the re-inscription of this unconscious knowledge into Consciousness. The implicit expectation is that the therapeutic effects will follow automatically. In this respect, Freud reveals himself as an inheritor of the Enlightenment, in his belief that the mere transmission of knowledge is enough to induce change. Nevertheless, beyond this Enlightenment, we meet Socrates with his insistent questions: what is knowledge, and how can it be passed on or taught? These are the two questions I want to address in this paper.

With respect to the first question, I have to specify that the knowledge concerned is rather particular: it is the knowledge that is searched for by every subject right from the start. The Dora case study illustrates the insistence and gives us the gist of this search: through her symptoms and dreams, Dora continually asks what it means to be a woman and a daughter in relation to the desire of a man (SE 7).

This particular illustration receives a general characterization when Freud begins to study childhood and thus discovers the generality of what he calls the infantile sexual researches—i. e., the original quest for knowledge. Just like the hysterical patient, the child wants to know the answer to three related questions. The first concerns the difference between boys and girls, the second question concerns the origin of babies, and the last question is about the father and the mother: what is their relationship? The child, says Freud, proceeds like a scientist and will forge genuinely explanatory theories, which is why Freud calls them infantile sexual researches and infantile sexual theories (SE 7: 194-97). The recurring problem with the knowledge produced is that the answers are never definitive, with the result that the questions persist. This was also the case with Dora, whose second dream mentions that “Sie fragt wohl hundertmal” (“She asks a hundred times”) (SE 7: 97). According to Freud, the infantile sexual researches falter on two specific points: the role of the father (“the fertilising role of the semen”) and the female sexual identity (“the existence of the female sexual orifice”), and this failure, says Freud, ends “in a renunciation which not infrequently leaves behind it a permanent injury of the instinct for knowledge” (SE 7:197). Instead of a correct knowledge, the child must content itself with the primary fantasies, combining true, false, and lack of knowledge into imaginary constructions. This, of course, will strengthen Freud's conviction that neurosis is either the effect of an incorrect knowledge in these matters, or the effect of a lack of knowledge.

Engaging the Question of Difference

We are beginning to appreciate that preparing beginning teachers for culturally diverse classrooms raises some surprisingly difficult questions for teacher education. In the first place, we lack much experience in educating for difference. The curriculum of teacher education has traditionally been structured around an array of commonalities of normal child development, learning theories, provincially mandated programs of studies, instructional planning procedures, and the identification and measurement of expected outcomes. It is a curriculum of sameness, aided and abetted by Lacan's “discourse of the university,” which demands a knowledge that is both certain and able to be exchanged from one who knows to one who does not. Given this tradition of conformity and the expectation of certainty, what are we to now say about cultural diversity in the preparation of teachers?

A second difficulty emerges when we actually try to address cultural difference in the teacher education classroom. Here we find that the absence of secure knowledge awakens the ambivalences of cultural identity among students in a context that is already fraught with the uncertainties of forming identities as teachers. Britzman has characterized the process of becoming a teacher as a time of “biographical crisis,” saying that learning to teach “is not a mere matter of applying decontextualized skills or of mirroring predetermined images; it is a time when one's past, present and future are set in dynamic tension” (Practice 8). For the student teacher faced with the fact of having to prepare to teach in contexts of cultural difference, the desire to teach and to be seen to be a teacher now becomes entangled with issues of cultural identity. We have found that this entanglement produces a highly charged emotional response from some student teachers in which heated arguments are liable to quickly erupt over rights, race, and redress in Canadian society. The fact that these topics come to the fore suggests that there is more at stake than we originally anticipated when we actively pursue teacher preparation for cultural difference.

Introduction: The Study of Burnout

Epidemiological research concerning burnout in educators (Wisniewski and Cargiulo) concludes that half of all teachers will leave the profession within 7 years. Yearly attrition rates among general educators have been estimated at 6 to 8% per year. Among special educators these yearly attrition rates are even higher. On average, special educators remain in the classroom for approximately 6 years. Needless to say, burnout is a major problem in educators and maybe in education in general.

In the mid 1970s a systematic interest began to be taken in the phenomenon of burnout. Burnout began to be studied both clinically (Freudenberger, “Staff”) and academically (e.g., Maslach). The flood of scientific publications that have since appeared is mainly of a quantitative and correlational nature. Much attention was paid to the connection between burnout on the one hand and many individual variables on the other hand. Integral conceptual models as well as systematic qualitative studies and longitudinal research data were relatively scarce. In the last decade a change has set in, however. There is now a wish to integrate burnout into wider theoretical frameworks and to apply theory-driven research.

In 1974 Herbert Freudenberger, a New York psychoanalyst, was the first to give burnout its psychological meaning.2 Freudenberger (“Staff,” “The Staff”; Freudenberger and Richelson) considered burnout as a kind of mental exhaustion caused by the effort to impose one's will in order to reach a goal. According to him it is a chronic condition caused by a gradual depletion of energy as a result of over-commitment. He observed that people prone to burnout are idealistic persons who don't want to give in to limitations. He states, “It is the overly dedicated and the excessively committed individual who will suffer” (“The Staff” 75). “They're burning out because they've pushed themselves too hard for too long. They started out with great expectations and refused to compromise along the way” (Freudenberger and Richelson 12). According to Freudenberger, persons working in the human service professions are especially prone to these forms of exhaustion. They expect to have an impact on the lives of others, but what they are confronted with is primarily their own powerlessness.

Democracy and Ambivalence: Totem and Taboo Revisited

Mark Blackell PHD

Mark Blackell

Mark Blackell   Candidate in Social and Political Thought at York University in Toronto, Canada. His dissertation examines the way in which select nineteenth-century liberal democratic thinkers view the democratic bond and portray the symptoms of modern democratic subjectivity.

In his essay “The Image of the Body and Totalitarianism,” Claude Lefort argues that totalitarianism is built upon the re-embodiment of democratic power at a symbolic level. At the end of the essay, imagining an interlocutor noting how his thoughts on embodiment are nourished by psychoanalysis, Lefort concurs and then adds:

But this connection is meaningful only if one asks oneself at which hearth Freud's thought was lit. For is it not true that in order to sustain the ordeal of the division of the subject, in order to dislodge the reference points of self and other, to depose the position of the possessor of power and knowledge, one must assume responsibility for an experience instituted by democracy, the indetermination that was born from the loss of the substance of the body politic? (Lefort 306)

Lefort's concluding remarks open up more questions than they answer. What is the relationship between psychoanalysis, as an inquiry into the divided nature of the psyche, and modern democratic subjectivity? How is psychoanalytic thought part of an inquiry into a problematic of the modern political subject more generally and of the modern democratic subject more specifically? Totem and Taboo, Freud's first substantial account of social, cultural, and political phenomena, provides a mythical narrative through which we can treat these questions. Totem and Taboo provides us with, I argue, an implicitly and inherently modern mythic narrative. Not only does the story of the primal crime at the core of Freud's narrative of the prehistory of civilization resonate with the modern democratic revolutions but its psychology is indebted to modern democratic political forms of society and subjectivity. In particular, Freud's story of the primal crime is an implicit story about a political revolution which revolves around the institutionalization of ambivalence in a way which helps us understand both the historical nature of psychoanalysis and the democratic unconscious.

Totem and Taboo as an Examination of the Political Institutionalization of Ambivalence

Totem and Taboo begins by drawing parallels between the mental lives of primitives and obsessive neurotics. Both are seen as setting up absolute prohibitions against taboo objects without apparent motive or obvious origin. Further, the taboo object easily contaminates other objects—often merely by touch—so that the prohibitions of both neurotics and primitives are easily displaced and various elaborate injunctions are established to perform cathartic or prophylactic ceremonies (Freud, Origins 80-81). Freud outlines these similarities so that he can then apply the psychoanalytically derived insight about neurotic prohibitions arising out of repressed desire to the prohibitions of primitive societies: the primitive's horror of incest is to be seen as a reflection of an unconscious desire to commit incest. These are, as Ricoeur suggests (201), essentially analogical applications of psychoanalytic conclusions to the mental life to primitive people. To be fair, Freud is aware of how little he has shed light on the social psychology of primitive peoples and that he is not yet saying anything about the distinctly social nature of the fear of incest, about its social institutionalization. He notes toward the end of the first chapter (Freud, Origins 69-70) that “all that I have been able to add to our understanding of [the primitive horror of incest] is to emphasize the fact that it is essentially an infantile feature and that it reveals a striking agreement with the mental life of neurotic patients.” There is not yet a distinct cultural theory of incest.

This article draws on interviews conducted by the author in July 1998 with Russian psychoanalysts and scholars, including members of the recently established East European Institute for Psychoanalysis in St. Petersburg: Dr. Mikhail Reshetnikov (the Institute's director), Dr. Alexander Etkind, and Dr. Viktor Mazin. The conference described in the article was hosted by the East European Institute and co-organized by the University of Florida's Institute for the Psychological Study of the Arts.

This essay is in part an attempt to imagine a connection between two disparate events: a Russian presidential decree of 1996 and a lavish party I attended on a houseboat on the outskirts of St. Petersburg on the 4th of July, 1998, as a participant in the 15th International Conference on Psychoanalysis, Art and Literature. Like other foreign speakers at the conference, I had arrived in St. Petersburg primed by Western press coverage of the endemic official corruption and gangster-capitalism that have bankrupted Russia's economy and polity following the collapse of communism in 1991—since when Russia's GNP has dropped by forty per cent; the national debt has risen to U.S. $140 billion; previously state-owned industries and services, including up to eighty-five per cent of banks, are now reportedly in the hands of organized crime; corporate and personal income taxes are largely uncollected; health and welfare systems are collapsing; wages and pension payments are in chronic arrears; and homelessness, beggary, suicide, and assassination rates are soaring. I was therefore surprised and intrigued to learn that in July 1996 Boris Yeltsin had found time to issue a presidential decree (No. 1044) entitled “On the Revival and Development of Philosophical, Clinical and Applied Psychoanalysis” in Russia. I knew that psychoanalysis had been officially suppressed by the Bolshevik Party in the 1930s, but surely, I thought, there must have been more urgent matters on Yeltsin's political agenda in 1996 than a government-sponsored revival of the highly individualized, private, expensive and hence elitist practice of psychoanalysis.

If an academic degree course in psychoanalytic studies does not give students access to the analytic profession, where can they acquire the knowledge and skills necessary for practicing psychoanalysis? If only psychoanalytic training institutes have the power to recognize and ratify the transition from apprenticeship to mastery, how do their assessment criteria differ from those routinely employed within modern universities? If psychoanalytic training is neither exclusively nor principally predicated upon the assimilation of psychoanalytic knowledge, does this entail that the process devalues traditional techniques of reading and writing? And if the transmission of psychoanalysis, conceived as the organized and controlled production of new clinicians, occurs through speech rather than writing, listening instead of reading, the signifier at the expense of the letter, logos to the detriment of gramme, how can an intrinsically irreplicable utterance contribute to the replication of an utterly transformative activity? If Lacan is right in postulating that “a letter always arrives at its destination” (Lacan, Purloined 53), doesn't this proposition imply that a signifier never arrives at its destination?

Partly culled from the mouths of ambitious graduate students, these questions raise a series of fundamental concerns spanning the entire history of the psychoanalytic movement. Talking cure rather than writing cure, psychoanalysis has elevated the principle of its alleged clinical success to the rank of a central criterion for selecting new recruits. Psychoanalysts are not born through reading and writing, but through speaking and listening. Blindness is perfectly compatible with psychoanalytic insight, yet the deaf-mute analyst (whether physically impaired or artificially deprived through the sensory limitations of a computer system) seems to constitute a contradiction in terms. From this vantage point, the academy could perhaps still try to educate its pupils as psychoanalysts by resuscitating the colloquia docta and the ancient practice of oral examinations, if only the learning outcomes were definable. Insofar as psychoanalysis deserves to be characterized as a “pedagogical experience,” a “process that gives access to new knowledge previously denied to consciousness” (Felman 76), the nature and status of this knowledge remains unclear. What is the assessor supposed to examine in an analytic candidate who decides to sit through the oral examination? Which, if any, questions did Freud ask and what was he trying to hear in the words of his potential collaborators? What did the applicants think about what Freud wanted to hear, implicitly or explicitly, in the meanderings of their speech? Knowledge instead of ignorance? Self-knowledge rather than psychoanalytic knowledge? Newly gained analytic self-knowledge as opposed to old and regular self-knowledge? And what if Freud, instead of examining anything at all, merely judged on the basis of his own likes and dislikes, whether those harbored for the actual candidates or for their own analysts?

An endorsement from Slavoj Žižek on the back of Henry's Krips' Fetish: An Erotics of Culture, suggests that the text is “arguably the best book on psychoanalytic social theory ever written.” In some ways the book might be considered a “reader's guide” to systematically understanding some of the more difficult concepts in Žižek. There is a careful and extended discussion of familiar themes: the fetishistic nature of ideology, the function of canned laughter, and the disavowal involved with a knowledge that is both affirmed and denied. There is also an original and smartly developed analysis of ideology and interpellation as effects that arise from a Lacanian conceptual ground: the objet a, the fetish, the gaze, pleasure, and repetition.

The fetish is a central concept for Krips, but it is one that exfoliates to explain an assortment of social practices. The first two sections of the book focus on a systematic understanding of the fetish. Krips begins this analysis with an extended discussion of Freud's grandson playing the Fort-Da game. For Freud, the fetish is a substitute for the mother's missing penis; for Krips, Lacan's conceptual framework shifts the fetish to a general structure of lack and disavowal. As a generalized human response to lack, the fetish does not function as a simple object. It is not a fantasy supplement useful to enable sex. Instead, the fetish functions within culture as a prop for a structural lack in the subject:

The fetish is a special instance of the objet a, one for which repression is breached to the extent that the subject more or less clearly recognizes the real source of his pleasure, and thus enters an economy of disavowal. In this way, the fetish is reconceived in a way that divorces it from its specifically Freudian meaning. (9)

Krips uses Lacan's discussion of Freud's Fort-Da discussion to illustrate. The grandson responds to his mother's absence by playing with a cotton-reel. Freud observes that the boy gains considerable pleasure by manipulating the reel by means a string.

Jeffrey Berman

Jeffrey Berman

Jeffrey Berman   Professor of English at the University at Albany. Imagine a university professor asking a student to reveal in class the most intimate details of a childhood trauma like sexual or physical abuse. We would all agree that such behavior would be shockingly unprofessional. And yet, every day in college classrooms and faculty offices across the country, students receive writing assignments requiring inappropriate self-revelation.

(Swartzlander, Pace, and Stamler)

The above passage, appearing in a 1993 issue of the Chronicle of Higher Education, reflects one of the most persistent criticisms of self-disclosing writing. The two-page article, entitled “The Ethics of Requiring Students to Write About Their Personal Lives,” warns of the potential psychological dangers of compelling students to write on intimate subjects and then grading the essays. Many of the article's concerns about personal writing are legitimate, but the authors present a distorted picture by focusing only on the risks and ignoring the many benefits of autobiographical writing. For example, they make no distinction between requiring and encouraging personal writing: neither is acceptable to them. They correctly realize that students are ambivalent about writing on painful or shameful topics but incorrectly assume that this ambivalence cannot be minimized or overcome. They do not trust students to write about traumatic experiences because of the fear that students will be retraumatized; the authors maintain that even if students choose to write about past victimization, they will not know how to observe appropriate boundaries and later regret their self-disclosures.

Some of the authors' arguments suggest reverse sexism. They envision the male professor as a wolf in pursuit of Little Red Riding Hood or as a Humbert Humbert obsessed with his nymphet Lolita. Their desire to protect female students from exploitation is commendable; yet in arguing that “required personal writing may particularly perpetuate the ‘chilly classroom climate’ for women, in which a complex of explicit as well as subtle behaviors creates an uncomfortable atmosphere,” Swartzlander, Pace, and Stamler seem to be unaware that women's studies courses have long emphasized the value of exploring personal aspects of education. As Cheris Kramarae and Paula Treichler noted (with the same meteorological metaphor) three years earlier, one of the reasons “women experience a ‘chilly climate’ in academic settings” is because of “curricula which largely exclude the experiences of women” (41). Swartzlander, Pace, and Stamler conclude with several recommendations to avoid injuring students, including writing assignments that are oriented more to the future than to the past, a recommendation that silences students about their own history.

Prophecies for Shabby Times

As the title suggests, in his recent book, Troubling Confessions: Speaking Guilt in Law and Literature, Peter Brooks examines the role of confession in American cultural and political life from the dual perspective of the legal and the literary worlds.

Given the popular confusion of confession with the analytic session, as well as the legal and literary aspects of several texts by Freud and contemporary work on psychoanalysis and the law, this book is of some interest. Its topic also appeals to the prurient in recent public discourse, and this is not a judgment of Brooks, for, like many Americans, he pays some attention to the confessional “moments” in the Monica Lewinsky-Bill Clinton sex scandal, thereby demonstrating the high/low pervasiveness of the confessional mode. Of course, Clinton's twelfth hour deal with the Independent Prosecutor, as well as his own slew of pardons, only further fills the air of public discourse with confessional words such as “admission,” “apology,” “forgiveness,” and “healing.”

Of course, there are more serious and dire examples of confession, notably the recent spate of state executions of murderers who allegedly confessed to their crimes. On August 7, 2000, the front page of the New York Times featured an article about mentally retarded inmates on death row, with special attention to the case of Oliver Cruz. Cruz's lawyer commented that given time his client would confess to almost anything—by August 9 Cruz was dead, executed by order of Texas Governor George W. Bush.

Brooks is the Chester D. Tripp Professor of Humanities at Yale University and a well-known figure in literary criticism circles. He is the author of many books, such as The Melodramatic Imagination, Reading for the Plot, and Body Work, and co-editor of Law's Stories: Narrative and Rhetoric in the Law.

This is the second in a series of articles whose aim is to bring psychoanalytic thought to bear on the problem of the death penalty in the United States. The general premise informing this project is that death penalty proponents want something from executions: that murder has taken something away from both the immediately affected people and the community at large and that execution of the guilty party will best redress the loss, best provide an optimal measure of satisfaction. Any pro-death penalty argument asserts that what is wanted from the execution of the convicted person is both achievable and legitimate—that the state, representing the people, has both reason and right on its side when it enacts a death sentence. Given the fact that the United States is alone among advanced industrial nations in not yet abolishing the death penalty, the enactment of death sentences here can be thought of as a local ritual. It is this local ritualistic dimension of the death penalty that puts the lie to any absolute ethical or material claims made by its proponents. Psychoanalysis has had a long history of addressing the determinants of local rituals and I lean on that tradition here.

Before proceeding, I want to summarize the first article in the series. In it, I addressed the two major arguments of death penalty proponents: (1) that execution is a better deterrent than other extreme forms of punishment, like life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, and (2) that execution's retributive dimension is a legitimate social necessity.

Since there is no evidence of the death penalty having a significantly differential deterrent effect, I argued that “its appeal to reason provides execution a rational cover, while its overt defiance of the evidence provides execution a robust, self-sustaining, vehicle for pre-rational action.” The search for retribution (sanctioned by the Supreme Court in 19761) informs this pre-rational action. This search is nested within an appeal for justice, closure, peace, etc.—each of which is treated as an attainable element of both private and collective rituals of mourning. The Kleinian Position: Phantasy, Splitting, and the Language of Psychic Violence

Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke

Simon Clarke   Faculty Research Fellow and Associate Director of the Centre for Psycho-Social Studies at the University of the West of England. His research interests include the interface between psychoanalytic and sociological theory; Kleinian and Post-Kleinian thinking; the social application of psychoanalytic theory and practice, and psycho-social research methods. He has published widely on the psychoanalytic understanding of racism and ethnic hatred and is currently completing a new textbook that explores psychoanalytic and sociological accounts of these phenomena. Simon can be contacted via e-mail at Simon.Clarke@uwe.ac.uk

Introduction

In previous papers (Clarke, “Splitting”; Clarke and Bird; Clarke, “Psychoanalysis”) I have explored the Kleinian concept of projective identification and related to it the problem of racism, arguing that it is central to our understanding of the visceral and embodied nature of hatred. This paper seeks to provide a more detailed analysis of the underlying mechanisms that shape human perception and human nature from a Kleinian object relations perspective. In the first section I introduce the reader to the Kleinian inner world of Phantasy and argue that it is an integral part of perception, the source of persecution on the one hand and stability on the other. Phantasy enables the ego to perform its most basic operation: the establishment of object relations. I then go on to discuss splitting as a mechanism of defense. Splitting for Klein is the most primitive form of controlling danger: separating good and bad. Splitting ranges from biological impulses to social constructions. The distinction between endangered and endangering is a biological impulse which enables us to flee, to separate ourselves from danger, but splitting is also part of the social organization and functioning of political systems. We therefore have the notion of a mechanism which originates in our primitive biology, and which has become synthesized within everyday interaction at a socio-political and group level.

The final section of this paper addresses the Kleinian position. The notions of position and projective identification are probably the most important contributions Klein has made to psychoanalytic theory and practice. Kleins notion of a position is crucial to her understanding of the development of the child. Her focus is the first year of life, in which we learn to deal with anxiety, terror, love and hate. I conclude by arguing that Melanie Klein's work addresses the harsh, cruel, and terrifying side of human nature (as well as the good), which some may call the reality of life. Taming the language of Klein would be tantamount to sweeping away this reality, for in Klein's notion of positions we have a theory which explains the dynamic nature of the human psyche within a social-relational context.

[[RunningHead]]

German Comedy, Part I: The Problem of American Scholarship

Edward Gamarra

Edward Gamarra

Edward Gamarra   Received a B.A. in psychology from Vassar College and an M.A. in Cinema Studies from NYU. Currently he is ABD at Emory University's Graduate Institute of the Liberal Arts, where he is writing a dissertation on comedy and perversion. His other articles cover topics ranging from cultural pathology to postmodernism, from the horror genre to Gen X sexuality. He is actively involved in the American Psychoanalytic Association's Subcommittee on Psychoanalytic Studies Programs and has been recently named assistant editor of JPCS.

In the West and perhaps globally, a number of gross generalizations about national character persist. The Irish drink. Pollacks are stupid. Snobbish Frenchmen shun obnoxious Americans. This brief report concerns itself with one of the most resilient and least contested examples of this genre of stereotyping: the humorless German. In the United States, mass media and popular entertainment perpetuate this conception of the German character as both agelastic (unable to laugh) and incapable of telling a joke (for the sake of simplification, I will equate “sense of humor,” “joking,” “humor,” and “comedy”). A recent beer commercial featured a stand-up comic stating, “I just flew in from Berlin and boy are my arms tired.” His monotonous voice and expressionless face are mirrored by an equally affectless audience. A stern Teutonic voice-over announces matter-of-factly, “Germans don't do comedy. Beck's beer … the best of what Germans do best.” Unlike other instances of ethnic humor, this particular stereotype has had a profound and detrimental impact on a cross-cultural understanding of national identity, specifically insofar as American scholarship has been infected by this biased image of Germanness. A cursory literature review reveals that Americans seem unable to conceive of Germans as funny people. A psychodynamic approach to German humor, or supposed lack thereof, helps rectify the dearth of critical commentary and provides insight as to why the stereotype persists.

My experiences as a graduate student exemplify the rampant generalizations and deep ignorance concerning German humor. During a course on “Early German Cinema,” I inquired about the impact of Chaplin, Keaton, and Harold Lloyd on the German film industry and the responses of German audiences. Further, had Germany produced any film comedies? Did it have a comedy subculture beyond cabaret's political satire? The genre was certainly overshadowed by indigenous critical emphasis and government-sponsored promotion of the Expressionist art cinema and the exaltation of directors like G.W. Pabst, Fritz Lang, and F.W. Murnau. My professor's response was, “I just don't know. I have never heard anything about it.” She then quipped that “Germans really don't laugh that much anyway.” In another class, “Weimar Culture, Weimar Film,” I posed similar questions. This time, the professor dismissively answered that the Germans “left comedy to the Americans,” and moved on.
